body.text: Nested data and a list of dicts: how web service responses look.

slides.title: Merging dictionaries
slides.main: The right dict wins: user settings override defaults.

slides.title: A dict from two lists
slides.main: zip makes pairs, dict turns pairs into a dict.

body.text:
names = ["Anya", "Boris"]
phones = ["111", "222"]
book = dict(zip(names, phones))
print(book)
Lists of different length: the longer tail is silently dropped.

slides.title: Dict comprehension
slides.sub: Key: value, then a loop, in braces
slides.main: Flipping a dict is one line; the values become keys.

slides.title: Grouping
slides.sub: A dict whose values are lists
slides.main: Create the bucket if missing, then add the item.

slides.title: setdefault
slides.main: A common pattern gets its own name: get with zero for counts, setdefault for groups.

body.text: Key exists: returns what is there. Missing: stores an empty list and returns it.

slides.title: Nested dicts
slides.sub: A dict in a dict: two keys in a row
slides.main: Reads left to right, like a file path; on untrusted data, use get at each level.

slides.title: List of dicts
slides.sub: The most common shape of tabular data
slides.main: Sorting by a field: pass key a function that pulls the field from a record.

body.text:
users = [{"name": "Anya", "age": 20}, {"name": "Borya", "age": 15}]
print([u["name"] for u in users if u["age"] > 18])

def get_age(user):
    return user["age"]

print(sorted(users, key=get_age)[0])

slides.title: Sorting a dict
slides.sub: Pairs get sorted, not the dict itself
slides.main: The key with the largest value in one line: max(d, key=d.get).

slides.title: Top most frequent
slides.main: Not one new keyword: the power is in combining techniques.

slides.title: Lookup table
slides.sub: A dict instead of an if / elif chain
slides.main: When branches boil down to "this: that", keep the table apart from the logic.

slides.title: Pitfalls
slides.sub: A shared list in the values
slides.main: fromkeys puts the same object under every key: references again.

body.text:
shared = dict.fromkeys(["a", "b"], [])   # one list for all
shared["a"].append(1)
print(shared)
Also: don't resize a dict in a loop (iterate over list(d)); the right dict overrides the left; normalize case and spaces.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: A dict + a list + a loop is already a data-processing language.
